title: Toasted Versus Charred Casks | Craft Beer School
desc: The difference between toasting and charring a whisky cask, what each does to oak flavour and colour and how distillers combine the two.
teaser: Toasting cooks the oak slowly. Charring burns it fast. They give a whisky very different flavours.
standfirst: Both toasting and charring use heat to change the inside of a cask, but they are different processes with different results. Wine casks are usually toasted. Bourbon barrels are charred. Many modern whisky casks get both. Here is how they differ and why it matters.
sections:
Toasting heats the inside of a cask slowly over a small fire, for many minutes, without letting the wood catch light. The heat penetrates the staves and cooks the wood. Charring sets the inner surface alight for well under a minute, leaving a black layer of charcoal. A char number 4, the heaviest common level, lasts only about 55 seconds.

Coopers already use a fire to bend staves into shape when raising a cask, so some toasting happens during building. A deliberate toast goes further and is controlled for time and intensity. Wine cooperages usually describe toast as light, medium or heavy. Our guide to cask char levels covers the numbered char scale.

Oak is made mostly of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin, plus extractives such as tannins and oak lactones. A slow toast breaks these down in a predictable order. Hemicellulose turns into sugars and caramel-like compounds. Lignin breaks down into vanillin and other aromatic compounds with spicy and sweet notes. With heavier toasting, smoky and roasted notes from compounds such as guaiacol begin to appear.

Toasting also reduces some of the harsher tannins and changes the oak lactones that give coconut notes, which heavy toasting lowers. The result is a cask with a deep layer of cooked wood that the spirit can draw from for years.

Charring creates the black surface layer, which absorbs some sulphur compounds and harsh notes from new make. Beneath it is a thin heated zone, sometimes called the red layer, where similar caramel and vanilla compounds form as in toasting, though over a shallower depth.

A purely charred cask tends to give quick colour, sweetness and a cleaner spirit. A purely toasted cask gives more depth of cooked oak flavour, spice and sweetness without the filtering effect of charcoal. That is why many cooperages toast first, then char on top. Bourbon barrels often get this treatment, which is part of why ex-bourbon casks bring so much vanilla to the Scotch whisky that fills them afterwards.
Wine casks, whisky casks and how they arrive

Wine barriques, usually 225 litres, are normally toasted and not charred, because wine makers want oak flavour without charcoal filtering. When a whisky distillery buys ex-wine casks for finishing, it is buying toasted oak with wine soaked into it. Some distilleries recondition those casks by shaving, retoasting and recharring them, which changes their character a lot.

Ex-bourbon casks arrive charred. Their char has already done much of its work on the bourbon. Sherry casks are usually toasted rather than heavily charred. Knowing the heat history of each cask helps you predict what it will do. Our guide on ex-bourbon, sherry and wine casks looks at those previous contents.
Choosing between them for your spirit

Think about what your new make needs. A heavy, sulphury spirit from short fermentations or worm tubs may benefit from charcoal to clean it. A light, delicate spirit may do better with a toast that adds sweetness and spice without stripping fruit. Many distilleries use a mix of both kinds of cask and blend the results.

In Indian heat both processes extract faster than they would in Scotland. A heavy toast or deep char in a small cask can add strong wood flavour within two or three years. Trials matter more than rules here. Fill the same new make into casks with different heat treatments and sample them every six months.

When you order, say clearly whether you want toast, char or both, plus the level. Ask the cooperage how they measure toast: by time, by temperature or by eye and colour. Ask for a cross section of a stave so you can see how deep the heat went. A good cooperage will explain the options and their likely flavour effects.

It also helps to ask how consistent the cooperage is from cask to cask. Two casks ordered at the same toast can differ if the fire, the wood moisture or the operator differs. Sampling a few casks from each delivery early on shows you how much variation to expect.

Designing a cask programme that matches your new make is one of the decisions that separates a whisky with a clear house style from one that tastes like whatever casks happened to be available.

Get two small offcuts of oak: one toasted, one charred. Put each in a jar with a little new make or neutral spirit diluted to around 60% ABV. Taste them after a week. The difference between the two jars is the clearest lesson in cask heat you will ever get.
faqs: What is the difference between toasting and charring a cask?
Toasting heats the wood slowly for many minutes without burning it. Charring sets the inner surface alight for less than a minute to create a layer of charcoal.
Usually not. Wine barriques are normally toasted, because winemakers want oak flavour without charcoal.
Can a cask be both toasted and charred?
Yes. Many cooperages toast staves first, then char the surface, especially for bourbon barrels.
